title: Japji 34–37, whole
tomorrow: how do you mint a word, like a coin, in a furnace?

lines: A MAP WITH A BOSS AT THE TOP.
cards: Simran's little cousin is on the couch playing a game with a map: world one, world two, a boss waiting at the top. The Japji's ladder has a top too, and pauris 34 to 37 draw the map. Five realms, five khands.

And at the kitchen table, two people Simran loves are reading her speech version. Her dad, Harjit, likes the line I worked hard to get here. Bebe taps the same line with one finger: and who gave you the strength?

teach.h: DHARAM KHAND: THE EARTH FOR RIGHT ACTION.
teach.b: Here's the map, paraphrased. First, Dharam Khand: nights, seasons and days, air, water and fire, and in the middle, the earth, set down as a place for right action. Here each of us is weighed by what we actually do.
Second, Gian Khand, knowledge: winds, waters and worlds without number, and the mind blazing as it takes them in.
Third, Saram Khand, which some read as the realm of effort and others as the realm of beauty; there, understanding is shaped. Fourth, Karam Khand, whose speech is power, home of the strong in spirit.

Fifth, Sach Khand, where the Formless dwells and watches with kindness, and Nanak says describing it is as hard as steel. Now the argument at Simran's table is an old one, and it lives inside one word.
Some Sikh readers hear karam as grace, a gift: the fourth realm isn't reached, it's given.

teach.h: SACH KHAND: HARD AS STEEL TO TELL.
teach.b: They point to how often the Japji says the door opens by the One's kind glance.
Other readers hear karam as action, the realm of deeds, and point to the map itself: the first realm judges what you do, and the third is shaped by effort.
Many hold both, work and gift on the same staircase. Simran doesn't cross out either line. She keeps I worked hard, and writes under it: and I was carried.

how: Pauris 34 to 37 are recited within the Japji each morning by Sikhs who keep Nitnem, and in katha, spoken commentary at the gurdwara, the five khands are often explained one realm at a time, with speakers giving different readings of saram and karam.

o: a hymn about the earth, said only at harvest
a rule about reading the Japji in five sittings
the stretch of the Japji that maps five realms

games.q: the map of the five realms — tap the pairs.
p: the earth set for right action

s: every translation gives the five realms the same names
saram is read as effort or as beauty, and karam as grace or as action.
in Dharam Khand the earth is set down as a place for right action
nights, seasons, days, air, water, fire, and in their midst the earth, for dharma.
the Japji says Sach Khand is easy to describe
Nanak says telling it is as hard as steel.

games.q: your dad says the Japji's top realms are climbed by hard work. you're asked to give the best case for the other reading. what do you say?
o: karam can mean grace: the Japji keeps saying the door opens by a kind glance.
effort is pointless, because the five realms are only pictures, not a path.
grace comes only once you've worked enough to deserve it, so work first.
games.why: some Sikh readers hear karam as grace, a gift; others hear action, the realm of deeds. many hold both. the best case for grace rests on the Japji's own talk of the kind glance.

practice: On a scrap of paper, write one line about something you worked hard for. Under it, write one line about what was given to you along the way: a teacher, a ride, a meal someone made.
Look at both lines for the rest of the sit, and leave them both standing.

wordCard.voice: Japji 34: the start of pauris 34 to 37, the five realms, from the earth set for right action to the realm of truth.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: a realm, a region. the Japji names five: Dharam, Gian, Saram, Karam and Sach Khand.

carryVoice: Hold onto this: the five realms, duty, knowledge, effort, grace and truth, with one word still argued over. Both lines stay in the version.

sources.ref: Ang 2, Japji, pauri 4 ('nadree mokh duaar': by the kind glance, the door), paraphrased
